Growth Foundations: Funnels, Metrics and Levers

Growth marketing treats the whole customer journey as one system you can measure and improve. In this module you map a real funnel with the AARRR model, find the stage that leaks most, choose a North Star metric backed by unit economics, and learn the growth levers that work in WhatsApp-first, trust-sensitive African markets.

A campaign asks: how many people did my advert reach? Growth marketing asks a wider question: **of everyone who heard about us, how many became happy, paying, returning customers, and how many brought friends?** It looks at the whole journey as one system, finds the weakest point, and fixes it with small, measured experiments. A business can double its sales without spending more on adverts if it stops losing people after they arrive.

This course assumes you already know marketing basics such as reach, click-through rate and UTM links. Here we go a level deeper: funnel analysis, unit economics, experiment design, honest statistics and selling growth work as a professional.

Turning a funnel into numbers

A funnel is only useful when every stage has a number for the same period, usually one month. Divide each stage by the stage before it to get the **step conversion rate**. The stage with a low rate and a cheap fix is usually your best opportunity, not automatically the stage with the lowest number.
Worked example: finding the leak in a meal-prep business

For example, Ada sells weekly meal-prep packs in Lekki, Lagos, through Instagram and WhatsApp. An average order is about ₦12,000 (illustrative). She pulls last month's numbers from Instagram Insights, WhatsApp Business labels and her Paystack dashboard.
Acquisition: 1,200 Instagram profile visits led to 300 WhatsApp chats. Step rate = 300 ÷ 1,200 = 25%.
Activation: 90 of the 300 chats became a first paid order. Step rate = 90 ÷ 300 = 30%.
Retention: 27 of the 90 first-time buyers ordered again within 30 days. Step rate = 27 ÷ 90 = 30%.
Referral: 9 of the 90 buyers sent a friend who ordered. Step rate = 9 ÷ 90 = 10%.
She models two fixes. Raising chat-to-order from 30% to 35% gives 300 × 0.35 = 105 first orders, 15 more per month, worth about 15 × ₦12,000 = ₦180,000.
Raising 30-day repeat from 30% to 40% gives 90 × 0.40 = 36 repeat buyers, 9 more per month, but each of those customers may keep buying for months, so the value builds up.
She reads 30 chats that did not convert. Most asked about delivery days and never got a clear reply. That points to a cheap fix: a quick reply with the menu, prices and delivery schedule.
Ada's first experiment targets activation (chat to first order) because she found a clear, cheap cause. Retention becomes her second experiment. She spent nothing on adverts to find this.
Look at people, not just percentages
Numbers tell you where people leave; conversations tell you why. Before you design any experiment, read at least 20 real chats, reviews or abandoned orders from the leaking stage.
Why growth teams obsess over retention

If customers do not come back, every naira spent on acquisition buys a one-time sale. When retention is strong, each new customer keeps paying, referrals rise because happy customers talk, and acquisition becomes cheaper over time. That is why experienced growth marketers check retention first: pouring adverts into a funnel that leaks after the first purchase is like filling a bucket with a hole in it.
**Healthy sign:** repeat buyers are a growing share of monthly orders.
**Warning sign:** sales only rise in months when you spend more on adverts.
**Fix order:** usually activation and retention first, then scale acquisition.
Set the window and the unit before you count

Two choices make funnel numbers comparable. First, the **time window**: use the same calendar month (or the same four weeks) for every stage, and keep it fixed when you compare later months. Second, the **unit**: count people, not actions. One customer who sends five messages is one chat, not five. If you mix people and actions, your step rates will look better or worse than they really are, and experiments built on them will aim at the wrong stage.

Write down where each number came from (Instagram Insights, WhatsApp labels, Paystack). Next month you must pull the figures from the same places in the same way, or a change in method will look like a change in performance.

Unit economics: is growth making or losing money?

Growth that loses money on every customer is not growth. Three numbers keep you honest. **Customer acquisition cost (CAC)** is what you spend to win one new customer: total marketing spend for a channel divided by new customers from that channel. **Lifetime value (LTV)** is the gross profit a customer brings over a period you choose, often 12 months: average order value × gross margin × number of orders in that period. **Payback period** is how long it takes for that customer's gross profit to repay the CAC.
Worked example: should Chioma scale Instagram ads?

For example, Chioma sells shea-butter skincare from Ibadan through WhatsApp. All prices are illustrative. Last month she spent ₦150,000 on Instagram ads and won 50 new customers. Her average order is ₦10,000 and her gross margin (after product and packaging cost) is 40%. Her records show a customer buys about 3 times a year.
CAC = ₦150,000 ÷ 50 = ₦3,000 per customer.
Gross profit per order = ₦10,000 × 0.40 = ₦4,000.
12-month LTV = ₦4,000 × 3 orders = ₦12,000.
LTV to CAC ratio = ₦12,000 ÷ ₦3,000 = 4 to 1.
Payback: the first order earns ₦4,000, which already covers the ₦3,000 CAC, so payback is on the first purchase.
She tests a micro-influencer channel: ₦90,000 brings 15 customers. CAC = ₦6,000. LTV to CAC = ₦12,000 ÷ ₦6,000 = 2 to 1, and payback needs 1.5 orders.

Instagram ads pay back immediately at 4 to 1, so Chioma can scale them carefully while watching CAC each week. The influencer channel is weaker; she keeps it small unless retention for those buyers proves higher.
About rules of thumb

Many investors use a rough guide that LTV should be about three times CAC or more. Treat it as a starting point, not a law. A business with little cash needs fast payback even more than a high ratio, because money spent on ads today must come back before stock needs restocking.
Common mistakes
Using revenue instead of gross profit for LTV, which can make a loss-making channel look healthy.
Dividing all spend by all customers, which hides a bad channel behind a good one. Calculate CAC per channel.
Counting returning customers as new, which makes CAC look lower than it is.
Assuming customers will buy for five years when the business is only one year old. Use the period you can actually observe.
CAC rises as you scale

The first customers from a channel are usually the cheapest. When you double the budget, CAC often climbs. Increase spend in steps (for example 20 to 30% per week) and recalculate CAC each time rather than assuming last month's figure still holds.
When payback takes several orders

Payback period is easy to calculate once you know CAC and gross profit per order: **orders needed = CAC ÷ gross profit per order**, then convert orders into time using how often customers buy. For example, if CAC is ₦8,000, gross profit per order is ₦4,000 and customers buy every two months, payback needs 2 orders, so about two to four months depending on when the first repeat order comes. During that time the business has paid for the customer but not yet earned it back, which ties up cash.

This is why a growing small business can run short of cash even when every customer is profitable in the long run. If you advise a client, show both numbers: the LTV to CAC ratio (is the customer worth it?) and the payback period (can the business afford to wait?). If payback is long, the best experiments are often in activation and retention, because they make the second order arrive sooner.
Recalculate LTV every quarter from real cohort data, not from hopes.
Keep a separate CAC for each channel and each month.
Share the inputs with the client so they can check your arithmetic.

The goal at each stage is unchanged; the route is shaped by trust, data cost and payment habits.
Lever 1: trust removes friction at activation
Show proof early: customer videos, delivery photos with permission, and your Corporate Affairs Commission registration number if registered (not to be confused with CAC, customer acquisition cost).
Offer a low-risk first step: a small trial size, pay-on-delivery within your city, or a clear refund rule.
Use a verified checkout link (for example Paystack or Flutterwave payment pages) so buyers are not asked to transfer to a personal account they cannot check.
Reply fast. A quick reply message with prices and delivery days often lifts first orders more than a new advert.
Lever 2: respect data costs

Heavy pages and long videos cost your customer money before they have bought anything. Keep landing pages light, compress images, offer a WhatsApp catalogue, and use short voice notes for explanations where customers prefer them. Every step you remove from the path to the first order is a possible activation experiment.
Lever 3: referral loops

A referral loop turns customers into acquisition. You measure it with the **viral coefficient (K)**: the average number of invitations each customer sends multiplied by the share of invitations that become customers. If K is 0.3, every 100 customers bring 30 more, who bring 9 more, and so on. When K is below 1 the loop amplifies your other channels rather than growing on its own, and the total from 100 starting customers is roughly 100 ÷ (1 − K).
Worked example: is the tutoring referral worth it?

For example, Funmi runs paid WAEC and JAMB revision classes for secondary school pupils, sold to parents through WhatsApp in Abuja. She plans to give each referring parent ₦2,000 off next term (illustrative), and only when the friend has paid.
She pilots with 100 parents. On average each shares the invite with 2 other parents.
15% of invited parents enrol. K = 2 × 0.15 = 0.3.
Extra customers from the loop: 100 ÷ (1 − 0.3) = about 143 in total, so about 43 extra parents over several cycles.
Cost: 43 discounts × ₦2,000 = ₦86,000, or ₦2,000 per extra customer.
Her paid-ad CAC is about ₦4,500 (from her own records), so referral customers cost less than half as much.
The referral programme is worth running. Funmi tracks K every term and tests whether a two-sided reward (both parents get ₦1,000 off) raises the share of invites that convert.
Protect customers and your budget

Pay referral rewards only after the new customer's payment clears, and cap rewards per person to stop people inventing fake accounts or referring themselves with a second number. Never ask customers for OTPs, PINs or card details on WhatsApp, and tell them publicly that you never will, because scammers copy popular referral offers.
Other levers worth testing
**Community:** a moderated WhatsApp group or Telegram channel for customers can lift retention when it shares useful content, not only adverts.
**Agents and ambassadors:** many fintech and FMCG brands grow through local agents paid per active customer; the same idea works for small brands with campus or market ambassadors.
**Timing:** test sending offers when your customers usually have money, for example soon after month-end salaries, and compare with mid-month.

Growth skills travel well. The same funnel and experiment methods apply whether you work for a Lagos fintech, a Nairobi e-commerce start-up, or remotely for a foreign company. What employers value is proof that you can find a leak, design a fair test and report the result honestly, which the rest of this course builds.
Measuring offline and word-of-mouth growth

Much referral in Nigeria happens offline: in markets, churches and mosques, office groups and family WhatsApp chats. You can still measure it. Give each customer a short personal referral code (for example AMAKA10) to share, ask every new customer "How did you hear about us?" with fixed options, and label the answer in WhatsApp Business. For ambassadors, give each a unique code or link so you can pay only for real paying customers.

Where many customers use basic phones or have little data, consider channels that work without the internet, such as SMS reminders sent with consent, phone calls for high-value orders, or partnering with a business that already offers USSD payments. Each of these is a test: measure the activation or repeat rate for customers reached this way against your usual channel before you invest more.

Cohort tables: the honest view of retention

A **cohort** is a group of customers who started in the same period, for example everyone whose first order was in January. A cohort table shows what share of each group is still buying in later months. It is more honest than total monthly sales, which can rise simply because you bought more ads while old customers quietly disappeared.
Worked example: did the loyalty change work?

For example, Ada (meal prep, Lagos) exports three months of paid orders from Paystack into Google Sheets. She adds a column for each customer's first order month. In February she introduced a free dessert on every fourth order.
January cohort: 80 first-time buyers. In February, 32 of them ordered again: 32 ÷ 80 = 40%. In March, 24 did: 24 ÷ 80 = 30%.
February cohort: 100 first-time buyers. In March, 45 ordered again: 45 ÷ 100 = 45%.
She compares like with like: month-1 retention was 40% for January and 45% for February.
She checks for other causes: no price change, no new ad channel, and February is not a holiday month for her customers.
She records it in her experiment log as "promising, not proven" because it compares only two cohorts and was not a controlled test.
Month-1 retention rose from 40% to 45% after the loyalty change. The cohort view shows the signal clearly; a controlled test (next lesson) is needed to be confident.

Write a hypothesis that can fail

Use this template: **Because we saw [evidence], we believe that [change] for [audience] will increase [metric] from [baseline] to [target] within [time].** A hypothesis that cannot be proven wrong ("better branding will help") is not a hypothesis. For example: "Because 18 of 30 lost chats asked about delivery days, we believe a quick reply with menu, prices and delivery days for new WhatsApp chats will raise chat-to-order from 30% to 36% within four weeks."
Prioritise: ICE and RICE

**ICE**, popularised by growth marketer Sean Ellis, scores each idea from 1 to 10 on Impact, Confidence and Ease, then averages the three. It is fast and good for small teams. **RICE**, published by the software company Intercom, is more careful: Reach (people affected per period) × Impact (3 massive, 2 high, 1 medium, 0.5 low, 0.25 minimal) × Confidence (as a percentage) ÷ Effort (person-weeks).
Worked example: ranking four ideas
For example, Ada has four ideas for her meal-prep business and one free afternoon a week to work on growth.
Quick reply with menu and delivery days: Impact 6, Confidence 8, Ease 10. ICE = (6 + 8 + 10) ÷ 3 = 8.0.
Free dessert on every fourth order: 7, 6, 6. ICE = 19 ÷ 3 = 6.3.
New Instagram ad creative: 5, 5, 7. ICE = 17 ÷ 3 = 5.7.
Build her own mobile app: 8, 3, 2. ICE = 13 ÷ 3 = 4.3.
RICE check on the top two. Quick reply reaches about 900 chats a quarter: 900 × 1 × 0.8 ÷ 0.25 week = 2,880.
Loyalty dessert reaches about 270 repeat-eligible customers a quarter: 270 × 2 × 0.5 ÷ 1 week = 270.
Both methods put the quick reply first. The app scores last because effort is high and evidence is thin, even though its imagined impact is large.
How big must the test be?

Small samples produce random swings that look like results. Before launching, estimate the sample you need. A widely used rule of thumb (Lehr's rule) for about 80% power at a 5% significance level is: **people per group ≈ 16 × p × (1 − p) ÷ d²**, where p is your baseline conversion rate and d is the smallest absolute change you care about. Online calculators such as Evan Miller's sample-size calculator give more exact figures.
Worked example: is this test even possible?
For example, Ngozi runs an online fabric store in Kano with about 1,800 product-page visitors a month and a 10% add-to-cart rate. She wants to test a new product-photo layout.
To detect a 2-point change (10% to 12%): 16 × 0.10 × 0.90 ÷ 0.02² = 1.44 ÷ 0.0004 = 3,600 visitors per group, 7,200 in total.
At 1,800 visitors a month, that would take 4 months, far too long.
To detect a 4-point change (10% to 14%): 1.44 ÷ 0.0016 = 900 per group, 1,800 in total, about one month.
She decides to test a bold change likely to move the rate a lot, not a small tweak.
Low-traffic businesses should test big, meaningful changes. Tiny button-colour tests need traffic most small businesses do not have.
A/B test or before-and-after?

**A/B test:** randomly split people into control (A) and variant (B) at the same time. Best evidence, because both groups face the same week, prices and news. Tools: Meta Ads A/B test feature, email platforms such as Brevo or Mailchimp, or alternating quick replies by chat order.

**Before-and-after:** change everything and compare with a previous period. Easier, but holidays, salary dates and competitor moves can fool you. Compare equal-length periods and note anything unusual.
Run one test per audience at a time, or you will not know which change caused the result.

Write the metric, the sample size and the end date in your experiment log before launching. Deciding these afterwards invites you to stop the test the day it looks good.

Reading results honestly: significance, guardrails and ethical growth
Check whether an A/B result is likely real using a two-proportion z-test

The most expensive mistake in growth is a false win: you believe a change worked, roll it out, and build on it, when the difference was luck. Honest reading of results is what makes your experiment log trustworthy to an employer or client.
Is the difference real? A simple significance check

For conversion rates, a **two-proportion z-test** compares two groups. Compute each conversion rate, the pooled rate p (all conversions ÷ all people), the standard error SE = √(p × (1 − p) × (1/n₁ + 1/n₂)), and z = difference ÷ SE. If z is above about 1.96 (or below −1.96), the difference is statistically significant at the 5% level. Free online A/B significance calculators do this for you; knowing the steps helps you spot a wrong claim.
Worked example: checkout page test
For example, Amaka tests a shorter checkout page for her Abuja kitchenware store. She randomly splits visitors for 14 days (two full weeks) and agreed the sample size in advance.
Control (A): 2,000 visitors, 100 purchases. Rate = 100 ÷ 2,000 = 5.0%.
Variant (B): 2,000 visitors, 130 purchases. Rate = 130 ÷ 2,000 = 6.5%.
She checks her guardrail: refund requests were 3 in each group, so no harm appeared.
The shorter checkout is a significant win at the 5% level, though only just. Amaka rolls it out and keeps watching purchase rate for the next month to confirm the lift holds.
Traps that create false wins
**Peeking:** checking daily and stopping the moment B looks ahead greatly raises the chance of a false win. Stop at the sample size and date you set.
**Too short:** run at least one full week, ideally two, so weekdays and weekends are both included.
**Seasonality:** Ramadan, Easter, December festivities, school resumption and salary dates change buying. Compare groups in the same period, not this month against last.
**Novelty effect:** returning customers may click a new design just because it is new. Check whether the lift lasts after two to four weeks.
**Many metrics:** if you check 20 metrics, about one will look significant by chance at 5%. Name one primary metric in advance.

Guardrail metrics

A **guardrail** is a metric that must not get worse while you chase the main one. Aggressive discounts can lift orders but cut gross profit; daily broadcast messages can lift clicks but increase blocks and opt-outs. Typical guardrails: gross margin, refund or complaint rate, unsubscribes or WhatsApp blocks, and delivery time.
Consent and the law

The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 requires a lawful basis, such as consent, for processing personal data, and gives people rights over their data. For growth experiments that means: message only people who opted in, make opting out easy, never buy or scrape contact lists, and tell customers how you use their data. The Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) oversees compliance.
Avoid dark patterns

Fake countdown timers, hidden fees added at checkout, pre-ticked consent boxes and fake "only 2 left" messages can lift short-term numbers while destroying trust. They also expose clients to consumer-protection complaints. Report them as unacceptable, not as clever growth hacks.
What to do with an inconclusive result

Many tests end with no clear winner. That is still useful information: it tells you the change does not have a large effect, so you can stop spending energy on it. Your options are to adopt the cheaper or simpler version if there was no harm, to run the test longer only if you planned that in advance, or to try a bolder variation of the idea. Do not keep extending a test until it happens to cross 1.96.

For example, Zainab owns a ready-to-wear brand in Abuja selling through Instagram, a website and WhatsApp. She says, "Our ads stopped working." You run a 45-minute discovery call and request view-only access.

Repeat orders within 60 days: 8%, down from her own earlier months, so retention also needs attention.

The ads were working better than Zainab thought; the problems were a slow landing page, missing WhatsApp attribution and weak retention. Your report recommends three experiments: a lighter landing page, a tracked WhatsApp link with UTM tags, and a post-purchase message series.

Employers and clients hiring for growth do not want a list of tools you have used. They want proof that you can find a leak, test a fix fairly and tell the truth about the result. Two or three well-written case studies do this better than any certificate.
The case-study structure
**Context:** the business, its customers and the goal (anonymise if the owner prefers).
**Baseline:** the funnel numbers and step rates before you started.
**Insight:** the evidence that pointed to the leak (for example 18 of 30 lost chats asked about delivery).
**Hypothesis and design:** the change, the metric, sample size, test type and dates.
**Result:** the numbers for each group, the significance check and guardrails.
**Decision and learning:** what was scaled or stopped and what you would test next.
Worked example: a one-page case study
For example, Ada's meal-prep business from earlier lessons agreed to be featured. Numbers are from her own records and are illustrative here.
Baseline: 300 WhatsApp chats a month, 90 first orders, chat-to-order rate 30%.
Insight: in 30 lost chats, 18 asked about delivery days and waited hours for a reply.
Test: new chats alternated between the old manual reply (A) and a quick reply with menu, prices and delivery days (B) for four weeks.
Result: A had 150 chats and 45 orders (30%); B had 150 chats and 60 orders (40%).
Decision: the lift is promising but not significant at 5%. Because the change is free and caused no complaints, she adopted it and kept measuring for another month.
This case study is strong precisely because it reports an honest, borderline result and a sensible decision. An employer sees judgement, not just a success story.
Failures belong in your portfolio
Include one experiment that did not work, with what you learned. It shows you can read data honestly, which is the rarest skill in growth work.

A roadmap turns the audit into a plan. Keep it to one page: the North Star and input metrics, the ranked experiment backlog, and a weekly rhythm. A common rhythm is a short weekly growth meeting: review last week's tests, decide, and launch the next ones.

Why this matters
From campaigns to growth systems
A campaign counts reach
Growth looks at the whole journey
Find the weakest point, fix it
Double sales without more ad spend
A campaign asks: how many people did my advert reach?

Growth marketing asks a wider question. Of everyone who heard about us, how many became happy, paying, returning customers who brought friends? It treats the journey as one system, finds the weakest point, and fixes it with small, measured experiments.
A business can double its sales without spending more on adverts, if it stops losing people after they arrive.
Five stages, each with a number
Acquisition: how do people find us?
Activation: a good first experience?
Retention: do they come back?
Referral: do they tell others?
Revenue: do we make money from them?

Every customer passes through five stages, nicknamed pirate metrics because the initials spell AARRR. Acquisition: how do people find you? Activation: do they have a good first experience, like a first order?
Retention: do they come back, say within 30 days? Referral: do they bring others?
Revenue: do you make money from them? For each stage, use the same month, and count people, not actions. One customer who sends five messages is one chat, not five.
Worked example
Ada finds the leak in her funnel
1,200 visits to 300 chats: 25%
300 chats to 90 first orders: 30%
90 buyers, 27 came back: 30%
Read 30 lost chats: delivery days unclear
Step rate = this stage divided by the stage before it.
For example, Ada sells meal-prep packs in Lekki, Lagos. Last month, 1,200 Instagram profile visits led to 300 WhatsApp chats. That is 25 percent.
90 of those 300 chats became a first paid order: 30 percent.
27 of the 90 buyers ordered again within 30 days, which is also 30 percent.
Each step rate is that stage divided by the stage before it. The best target is a low rate with a cheap fix, not simply the smallest number.

Numbers show where people leave. Conversations show why. Ada reads 30 chats that did not convert. Most asked about delivery days and never got a clear reply. A quick reply with menu, prices and delivery schedule is her cheap first experiment.
Unit economics
Should Chioma scale Instagram ads?
For example, Chioma sells shea-butter skincare from Ibadan and won 50 new customers from ads.
Instagram ad spend
CAC: cost per new customer
Gross profit per order
12-month LTV, 3 orders
All prices are illustrative.
Growth that loses money on every customer is not growth. For example, Chioma sells shea-butter skincare from Ibadan. Last month she spent 150,000 naira on Instagram ads and won 50 new customers.
Customer acquisition cost, or CAC, is spend divided by new customers from that channel: 3,000 naira each.
Her average order is 10,000 naira with a 40 percent margin, so each order earns 4,000 naira gross profit. Customers buy about 3 times a year, so lifetime value, or LTV, is 12,000 naira.
That is 4 to 1, and her first order already pays back the CAC. She can scale carefully, watching CAC every week.
Honest numbers vs flattering numbers
Do
Use gross profit for LTV
Calculate CAC per channel
Use the period you can observe
Raise spend in steps
Don't
Use revenue for LTV
Divide all spend by all customers
Count returning customers as new
Assume CAC stays the same

Use gross profit, not revenue, for LTV. Calculate CAC for each channel separately. Use only the period you can actually observe. And when you scale, raise spend in steps, for example 20 to 30% per week.
Using revenue can make a loss-making channel look healthy. Mixing channels hides a bad one behind a good one. And CAC often climbs when you double the budget, so recalculate each time.
Local growth levers
Levers that work in Nigeria
Show proof early, offer a low-risk first step, use a verified checkout link, reply fast.
Light pages, compressed images, a WhatsApp catalogue, short voice notes.
K = invites per customer x share who buy. Reward only after the friend pays.

Many Nigerian customers pay per megabyte, prefer transfer or pay-on-delivery, and have been burned by fake vendors. So the first lever is trust: customer videos, a trial size, a verified payment page, and fast replies.
The second lever is respect for data costs. Every heavy page or long video costs your customer money before she has bought anything.

The third is a referral loop. For example, Funmi's tutoring parents each share an invite with 2 others, and 15% enrol. K is 0.3, so 100 parents bring about 43 extra, at 2,000 naira each, less than half her ad CAC of 4,500 naira.
Safety
Pay rewards only after payment clears
Cap rewards per person
Never ask for OTPs, PINs or card details
Say publicly that you never will
Scammers copy popular referral offers. Warn your customers.
Pay referral rewards only after the new customer's payment clears, and cap rewards per person, so nobody invents fake accounts or refers herself with a second number.
Never ask customers for OTPs, PINs or card details on WhatsApp, and tell them publicly that you never will, because scammers copy popular referral offers.
Key points
Remember
AARRR: five stages, each with a number
Pick the leak with a clear, cheap fix
CAC = channel spend / new customers
LTV = order x margin x orders
Check retention before scaling ads

To remember. Measure all five stages. Fix the leak with a clear cause and a cheap fix. Check LTV to CAC and payback for each channel. And check retention before you pour money into ads, or you fill a bucket with a hole in it.

Track, test and read results honestly
Track, test, and read your results honestly.
This is the video for module two of Growth Marketing.
Why this matters
The machinery of growth
You cannot improve what you cannot see
Most ideas fail, so test them on purpose
A false win is the costliest mistake
You cannot improve what you cannot see, so first you set up simple tracking.
Most growth ideas fail. A professional chooses each test deliberately, designs it to give a clear answer, and records it.
And the most expensive mistake is a false win: believing a change worked when the difference was luck.
Your growth stack
Free tools that cover every stage
GA4 for website events
Meta tools and Instagram Insights
WhatsApp Business labels
Google Sheets: funnel, cohorts, experiment log
Google Analytics 4, or GA4, records website events such as add to cart and purchase. Meta tools and Instagram Insights show reach, clicks and cost per result.
WhatsApp Business labels count new chats, paid orders and repeat buyers. Payment exports give real paid orders by date.
Google Sheets holds it all together. Use the same lower-case spelling in every UTM link, or Instagram and IG become two sources.
Cohort tables
Ada checks her loyalty change
January: 80 first-time buyers
February: 32 came back, 40%
February cohort: 100 buyers
March: 45 came back, 45%
Log it: promising, not proven
A cohort is a group of customers who started in the same month. It is more honest than total sales, which can rise with more ads while old customers quietly leave.
For example, Ada in Lagos had 80 first-time buyers in January.
In February, 32 of them ordered again. That is 40 percent month-1 retention.
In February she added a free dessert on every fourth order. Of February's 100 first-time buyers, 45 came back in March: 45 percent.
She checks for other causes, finds none, and logs it as promising, not proven, because it was not a controlled test.
The experiment loop
Because we saw: 18 of 30 lost chats
We believe: a quick reply with delivery days
Will raise: chat-to-order 30% to 36%
Within: four weeks
Fix the metric, sample size and end date before you start.
Use this template: because we saw this evidence, we believe this change will raise a metric from a baseline to a target, within a time.
For example: because 18 of 30 lost chats asked about delivery days, a quick reply with delivery days...
...will raise chat-to-order from 30% to 36% within four weeks. Better branding will help is not a hypothesis. It can never be proven wrong.
Write the metric, the sample size and the end date in your log before launching. Otherwise you will be tempted to stop the day it looks good.
Prioritise
ICE scores rank Ada's ideas
Test first
Quick reply: ICE 8.0
Free dessert: ICE 6.3
New ad creative: ICE 5.7
Test last
Her own mobile app: ICE 4.3
High effort
Thin evidence
ICE scores each idea from 1 to 10 on Impact, Confidence and Ease, then averages them. Ada's quick reply scores 6, 8 and 10, an ICE of 8.0. The dessert scores 6.3, a new ad 5.7.
Building her own app scores 4.3. Its imagined impact is large, but effort is high and evidence is thin. RICE, which adds reach and effort in person-weeks, also puts the quick reply first.
Sample size
Low traffic? Test big changes
Per group = 16 x p x (1 - p) / d squared
10% to 12%: 3,600 per group, 4 months
10% to 14%: 900 per group, one month

Small samples swing randomly and look like results. A rule of thumb for the people you need per group is 16, times your baseline rate, times one minus that rate, divided by the change you care about, squared.
For example, Ngozi's fabric store gets about 1,800 visitors a month, with a 10% add-to-cart rate. To spot a change to 12% she needs 3,600 per group. That would take 4 months.
To spot a change to 14% she needs only 900 per group, about one month. So she tests a bold change, not a tiny button colour.
Reading results
Trustworthy
Sample and date fixed in advance
Different periods compared
Winner picked from many metrics

For example, Amaka tests a shorter checkout for 14 days. A gets 100 purchases from 2,000 visitors, 5.0%. B gets 130, 6.5%. Her z value is about 2.04, just above 1.96, so it is significant at the 5% level. Refunds stayed at 3 in each group.
Be suspicious of a test stopped the moment B looked ahead, one that ran only a few days, or one comparing this month with last. And name one main metric in advance.
Ethical growth
Protect customers while you test
Watch gross margin, refunds and complaints, opt-outs or blocks, and delivery time.
Message only people who opted in. Easy opt-out. Never buy or scrape contact lists.
No fake countdowns, hidden fees, pre-ticked boxes or fake only 2 left messages.
A guardrail is a metric that must not get worse while you chase the main one. Discounts can lift orders but cut profit. Daily broadcasts can lift clicks but bring blocks.
The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 requires a lawful basis, such as consent. Keep customer sheets private, and never post screenshots showing customer numbers.
And avoid dark patterns. They lift short-term numbers while destroying trust.
Key points
Remember
Track every stage; build a cohort table
A hypothesis that can fail
Rank ideas with ICE or RICE
Fix sample and end date; do not peek
Guardrails, consent, no dark patterns

To remember. Track every stage and read retention by cohort. Write a hypothesis that can fail, and rank ideas before testing. Fix the rules in advance, do not peek, and protect customers while you grow.

Audit, price and prove your growth work.
This is the video for module three of Growth Marketing.
Why this matters
Turn the method into paid work
Clients say: sales are slow
Your first job is diagnosis
Price so you never work at a loss
Prove skill with honest case studies
Clients rarely say, please fix my activation rate. They say sales are slow, or our ads stopped working. Your first job is diagnosis.
In this module you run a growth audit, price and scope the work so it stays profitable, and package your experiments into case studies that win clients or a growth role.
Discovery
Questions for the discovery call
Goal: what would make 90 days a success?
Customers: who buys, why, why do they leave?
Funnel: first contact to payment
Data: what is tracked, who can export?
Resources and past tests

A growth audit is a short, fixed-scope project: a baseline funnel, the tracking gaps, and three recommended experiments. It starts with a discovery call. Ask: what would make the next 90 days a success?
Ask who buys most often, why they choose you, and why people leave. Then map what really happens between first contact and payment.
Ask what is tracked today and who can export it, what budget and help there is, and what they have tried before.
Talk for less than a third of the call, and summarise back what you heard.
Safety
Lowest role that works, e.g. Viewer
CSV export of payments, not a login
Agree in writing how data is stored
Remove access when the project ends
Never accept a client's personal passwords or OTPs.
Ask to be added with the lowest role that works, such as Viewer in Google Analytics, and take a CSV export of payments rather than a dashboard login.

Agree in writing what data you will see and how you will store it, and remove access at the end. Payment exports are personal data under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, so keep them in a protected account with two-step verification.
Never accept a client's personal passwords or OTPs. Role-based access protects both of you.
Worked example
Zainab's ads were working after all
6,000 clicks, only 2,100 sessions
Slow home page on mobile data
45 WhatsApp orders never counted
True CAC about 2,860 naira, not 5,000
For example, Zainab owns a ready-to-wear brand in Abuja and says her ads stopped working. Last month her ads got 6,000 link clicks, but GA4 shows only 2,100 sessions.
About two-thirds of clicks never load the site. On a mid-range phone, the home page is slow on mobile data.
The website had 60 orders, but 45 more came through WhatsApp chats, and these were never counted as ad results.

So her 300,000 naira of ads brought 105 orders. True CAC is about 2,860 naira, not the 5,000 she calculated. The ads were fine. The leaks were a slow page, missing WhatsApp tracking and weak retention.
Pricing
Kemi prices an audit
For example, Kemi, a growth marketer in Port Harcourt, sets her own rate at 15,000 naira an hour.
20 hours of audit work
Plus 15% buffer: the quote
50% deposit before work starts
Her own illustrative figures.
Price from your own numbers, built from what you need to earn, the hours you can bill, and your costs. For example, Kemi sets her rate at 15,000 naira an hour.
She estimates 20 hours: the discovery call, data cleaning, the funnel and cohort work, the report, and the presentation. That is 300,000 naira.
She adds a 15% buffer for revisions and delays, and quotes 345,000 naira for a three-week audit.
She takes 50%, which is 172,500 naira, before work starts, and the rest on delivery of the report.
Proposals and scope
Protect yourself and the client
Do
List exact deliverables and dates
List exclusions, like ad spend
Quote extra work in writing
Keep a fixed base fee
Don't
Guarantee a growth percentage
Accept pay only if sales grow
Start before payment arrives
Refund a client's overpayment

Your proposal lists exact deliverables, dates, what the client must provide, and exclusions, such as ad spend and paid tools. When a client asks for more, reply warmly: happy to help, I will send a short quote.

Never promise a growth percentage. Growth depends on stock, delivery and the owner's speed. And beware of new clients who overpay and ask for a refund of the difference. Confirm money has reached your account in your banking app before starting.
Case studies
Ada's honest case study
Baseline: 300 chats, 90 orders, 30%
Insight: 18 of 30 lost chats asked delivery
Test: A 30% vs B 40%, 150 chats each
z about 1.82: promising, not significant
Decision: free, no complaints, adopted

Employers want proof you can find a leak and tell the truth about the result. For example, Ada's case study starts with her baseline: 300 chats, 90 first orders, 30 percent. The insight: 18 of 30 lost chats asked about delivery days.
For four weeks, new chats alternated between the old reply, A, and a quick reply, B. A converted 30 percent, B 40 percent.
But z is about 1.82, below 1.96, so it is not significant. Because the change was free and caused no complaints, she adopted it and kept measuring.
This case study is strong precisely because it is honest.
Key points
Remember
Sell a fixed audit first
Count every channel before judging CAC
Price = hours x rate + buffer
Never guarantee growth
Include borderline and failed results

To remember. Sell a fixed audit first, and count every channel, including WhatsApp orders, before judging CAC. Price from hours, rate and buffer, and take a deposit. Never guarantee growth. And report results honestly, including the ones that failed.
